Expectation1: Help out during difficult times or emergencies.
Situation1: You get a frantic call from your friend whose car has broken down on the side of the highway late at night, and they need you to come get them immediately.
Expectation2: Teach Torah and Jewish law to children and adults.
Situation2: An optional, drop-in adult education class on a general topic is scheduled.
Story:
My phone buzzed just as I was reviewing my notes for tonight’s adult education class at the synagogue. It was late, and the class was optional, but I knew a handful of regulars would be there, expecting me to guide them through the week’s Torah portion. I glanced at the clock—fifteen minutes until I needed to leave. Then my phone rang again, this time with a frantic call from my friend David. His car had broken down on the highway, miles from town, and he sounded scared. “Can you come get me? I don’t know who else to call,” he pleaded.

As a friend, I felt the pull to rush to his side, to be the person he could count on in a crisis. But as a rabbi, I knew my students would be waiting, some of them coming just for the comfort and insight our sessions provided. My mind raced with the weight of both expectations—David’s urgent need for help, and my community’s trust in my presence and teaching. I stood in the hallway, keys in hand, heart pounding, torn between two worlds that both needed me right now.
